utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness, dear colleague. I have a few more documents to look at briefly. I think that I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's just say that document P475.1 and document P629.1 and P740.1 are missing from these binders, although they are on this list, on this summary. However, we haven't received them so we just wish to draw the attention of the Honourable Trial Chamber to that as well. You probably haven't received copies of these documents either. So I'm not going to put any questions regarding those documents. Let us start with document 241 -- actually, I assume it is document 241, but it's in binder number 3. Oh, sorry, I didn't realise you haven't got it yet. Armed conflict number 3. And it has to do with Exhibit 886. Madam Registrar, it has to do with 886, that binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't have it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think it has anything to do with the third binder. It should be in the chronological binders. It's simply 886 in the binder, in the 17 binders that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with volume 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you mean the list, the list of those documents in volume 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the documents in a logical sequence, according to 886, and I have a separate binder, and I thought that you did too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I think we are going to have some difficulties now. This is document P241.1. I don't know which binder this is in now. Yes. It's from those 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, let me make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it should be -- I don't think it's up to the Prosecution to find the documents for the Defence, but they are in binder number 6. It's in binder number 6, 241.1, and it is in my binder. I'm looking at it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In my binders, I only have 241 rather than 241.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my document is marked 241 as well. There is no .1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Line 13 on page 2, counsel specifically said 241.1, so that's what I was responding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Distinguished colleague, I think that it is some kind of a misunderstanding. I only talked about the documents that were missing. Those documents had .1. But this particular document is only 241. And the first documents that I mentioned, the three documents that are missing that were put forth by you all have a .1 at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know whether you have these documents in front of you. Yes, you will be getting them. All right. Witness, I have just one question with regard to this. How is it possible to do the translation on the basis of this copy? Because in the Croat original, you absolutely cannot see a thing, absolutely nothing. This is the -- a copy of the Croatian original that I have. Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, that's not an appropriate question for this witness. The witness didn't provide the translation. If counsel has a problem with the copy, he could have asked me for an additional copy. These documents were provided some time ago. If counsel had approached me and asked for a better copy, we would have certainly sought to do that. So if counsel wants to complain to me about the copy he was provided, I am happy to have him do so. I'm happy to respond. But it's not a question for this witness, Your Honour. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I agree with you, but we also share the same problem with Defence counsel. We have three pages attached following the document, and the one page is quite illegible, and the other two are just blank paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take the Chamber's comment as a request, and I will respond to it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assume that none of my questions are right from the point of view of the Prosecution, but I would like to say the following to my learned friend. We got this abundance of documents, and we requested extra time to look at them, and I did not know what would be tendered into evidence. And I did not, therefore, know what I should note and what I should not, and that's why I think that these remarks were inappropriate. It is totally illegible. I have no questions with regard to this document because I have no idea what it's about and I cannot match it to the original, so then I'm just going to move on to the next document, 364.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have two questions in this regard. What's the source of this document? Does it belong to milinfo 005 or something else? There is no signature; we can't really see anything. And on the last page, this military unit, what does this belong to?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand. This is a document -- sorry -- of the same kind that we discussed yesterday, and I will -- all what I can tell is what I already said yesterday. We discussed a similar document also produced by BritBat. So the information available to me is that this was submitted by the British forces, that this seems to be an internal report, and that is why it doesn't have signature or stamp. I can tell you that milinfo is the general denomination for these kind of reports produced by the British battalion, milinfosum, as you can see. PWO is one of the names of such British battalions, the same as yesterday we saw the Cheshire denomination. Here, this is -- I believe it's Prince of Wales. I don't know what the O stands for, but that was the name of such battalion. I believe that this is an acceptable document because we have interviewed a significant number of officers of the British battalion from the commanders, the top commanders of the battalion, to the liaison officers, intelligence officers, and -- well, I would say a number of officers involved in the production of such reports; and our experience is that they are objective sources, that they reported objectively and that the reports are credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I still have not understood whether this report belongs to milinfo 005.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see in the heading. It says, "milinfo 006," right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. But now look at the other page, the last sentence, [In English] "... to milinfo 005."

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, I believe that the logical explanation for this is that they missed -- they eventually forgot to attach this to the previous report and they are attaching it to the next one, to number 6. That's what it says here, "The missing annex to milinfo 005 is contained as an annex to this report." That's what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My understanding was different, that this drawing on the other page is an annex to 005. Now, tell me, what does this drawing pertain to, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. Again we are having comments and argument by counsel. The document speaks for itself. The witness has already answered. He simply read what it says on the bottom of page 2, and then we just, again, have this continuing series of arguments with the witness. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not arguing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we also want to know what this means and how it's attached to this document. We would like to hear the explanations from this witness, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have absolutely no objection to the witness providing as much insight on the attachment of the 303 Brdska Brigada if that can assist the Chamber. In terms of how it became attached to the -- this particular milinfosum, I'm at a loss to any mystery in the courtroom. The document says quite clearly on the bottom of page 2 why it's attached to the document. I don't see any mystery about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There is no controversy on this. We agree. There seems to be a drawing that should have been attached to milinfo number 5, but for some, I understand, I guess - I can only guess - some human mistake, it ended up added to the next report, to the report number 6. That is what the document itself says. As far as I can see, actually, report 6 does not refer to this unit. Most likely, report 5 would contain some information related to this unit. I am not familiar with this unit. I cannot assist you much with this. I can see here that here it says, in the original, in Bosnian language, 3rd Corps, which is certainly a denomination of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 3rd Corps, I believe, was the corps deployed in Central Bosnia. That is as much as I can tell you. Most likely this refers to certainly a Bosnian unit from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly, then, that this other page of this document, together with this drawing, comprises a single entity and has nothing to do with page 1 of that document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is my understanding, following what the document states at the bottom of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Your Honour, if you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I wonder whether you could assist the Chamber. We found that those British government documents are very peculiar. We need some corroboration concerning those documents. Are you going to call some more witnesses of the British army, or are you going to provide us more documents to support those documents you tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm glad you asked that question. I'm glad to have the opportunities to address this because I was thinking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about this this morning. Your Honour, the uncontradicted state of the testimony right now, the only evidence in this case -- the only evidence in this case is the uncontradicted testimony of this witness that these documents were provided by the British government. That's not contested. We agree it doesn't say -- doesn't have a signature, doesn't have a stamp, for the reasons this witness has already explained. That's also uncontradicted. So I'm at a bit of a loss as to what more we can do on that. If someone questions that it didn't really come from the British government, I will be happy to contact the British government and have a witness come from the British government who can say, "These are our documents," if that's the Chamber's concern. But, Mr. President, we know the Office of the Prosecutor has an extensive record-keeping system. What this witness did, and what he has said several times now since he began testifying last week, that we can go to our records, we can go, we look up this number, 00274020, we go back in our records, we can find when it was provided, where it was provided from. It came from the British government. That's uncontradicted. That is the state of the evidence in this case. There is no reason, respectfully, to question that. Until counsel raises some question, puts that assertion in doubt - there has not been one, I submit - then the state of the evidence is this is a document provided by the British government. If the Chamber wants me to provide additional information, I will certainly do that. I will certainly follow the Court's direction, obviously. This is -- there is a large volume of these documents that have been provided in the Central Bosnian cases, probably by the hundreds, in the Kordic case, in the Blaskic case, just like the Spanish battalion did INTREPS and INTSUMS, the British army calls this similar document, their daily reports, a milinfosum which is an abbreviation for "military information summary." This particular brigade, which had its tour of duty in Central Bosnia in the first six months, approximately, of 1993 was the Prince of Wales Own. Just like the Canarias Group and just like the Malaga Task Force, they were a British army battalion that was assigned peacekeeping duties in Central Bosnia. They made daily reports. They didn't sign their reports. They made them just like this, and they were admitted by the hundreds in the Kordic and Cerkez case and in the Kordic case -- excuse me, in the Blaskic case, and in a number of other -- and in Kupreskic, and in virtually every Central Bosnia case. So that -- I can provide the Chamber with that additional information. If the Chamber wishes me to call a representative of the British government, I will only be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In fairness to the Defence counsel, and in the interests of justice, we will require you to provide us any additional information concerning those documents. And if possible, you may call a witness from the British army. Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to Document P419. Witness, before that, can I ask you whether you wrote this summary or -- these summaries or, rather, do you know who wrote them, these summaries accompanying the exhibits? Have you written that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you because with regard to this particular document - and there are several such documents - somebody has been claiming that this is somebody's signature, and it has nothing to do with the document actually. So I hope you understand why I asked you this. And on the other hand, it has been tendered. For example, this Document 429, it says that it was -- I'm sorry, made a mistake. This is Document 419, that it was signed by Zeljko Bosnjak. And now, please look at the Croat original and look at the signature. Of course, all of us coming from the Croatian area, first of all, see that somebody signed this paper for him, and that the signature certainly does not correspond to Zeljko Bosnjak. We will have other such problems, too, however, since this was tendered, I am a bit concerned. So could you please look at the Croatian original. And at first glance, does this look like the signature? Of course, you're not a signature expert. I'm not going to tire you with this much longer, but I think this is quite evident, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can agree with this. It is actually not necessary to look at the original because that shows in the translation as well. The translation says "For Zeljko Bosnjak," meaning that someone else signed for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that we haven't got any of these documents, and it's very difficult to work that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I don't think that there is no misunderstanding really. This is what it says in P886, and it coincides with the document. I just hope that there is no misunderstanding between us. That's what I'm trying to say. And my next question is --

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me qualify. Normally, this may happen, this actually happens in many documents. It's a normal occurrence in any organisation. We normally explain these, making a distinction between type-signed and hand signed. So it can be also said or explained this, that the document was type-signed by Zeljko Bosnjak, because you can see that his name is typewritten, but this is a minor qualification. Essentially, I can agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my next question, how did you conclude that this is the stamp of the Convicts Battalion? Because in the original that I have, you can't see what the stamp says at all, or whether it says the Convicts Battalion stamp at all.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in the copy that I have, I can't see Convicts Battalion written. I can see Department of Defence, right, and Convicts Battalion is mentioned in the body of the text as well as in the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We can read the text. We can read that the commander of the Convicts Battalion - all of this is typed, without the signature - is Zeljko Bosnjak. What I was asking about, however, is the stamp.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is that, indeed, the stamp is partly illegible, almost totally illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Let us move on to the next document, 429. I think it follows the sequence.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... qualification to understand how this goes. The documents that you see with the ERN number, they are all kept in a CD format. When we want to retrieve a document, we have to print it from a CD, from a compact disk, and then we have to make a photocopy. So in the process of copying or reproducing, the quality may deteriorate. What happens in many cases - this may be the case in other cases - is that the original is sufficiently good to read it and to translate it. But in some copies, it deteriorated and, in fact, you cannot read that. In many cases that can be solved, making an effort to print a better copy, to provide with a better copy. That's a technical problem that in most of the cases can be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I agree with you, you know, but this is being tendered as evidence; and if you have the originals, why aren't they put in a special separate binder so that we can have a look at them? That's why I'm asking these questions of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, that is not a question for the witness. If Mr. Krsnik would like to contact me out of court, I would be happy to discuss these matters with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I think all those questions could be solved outside this courtroom. We should make the best use of time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. However, I absolutely disagree with my learned friend from the Prosecution. He is now inviting me to cooperate regarding the documents that he is tendering and on which we spent weeks of work and which are about to be admitted which are also outside of my control. And when I'm pointing out the deficiencies in these documents, he is inviting me to cooperate better. It's not as if he has given us enough time to prepare in advance. This is not an early stage of study of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you have to know that this witness - he, himself - did not prepare those binders. The question you asked is why aren't they put in a special separate binder so we could have a look at them. I think preparing the binders is the job of the Prosecutor, rather than this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree absolutely, Your Honour. But look, why is something being claimed here that cannot be seen from the document? It doesn't follow from the document. On Exhibit P886, certain claims are made and are also tendered as evidence, and we don't have a document that confirms that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, once again, Mr. President, counsel just said a moment ago that they have been working on these documents for some weeks. That was counsel's own words. I would have been only too happy if he had contacted me in the past two weeks to obtain a better copy. I object to the procedure by which counsel works with the documents for weeks, doesn't approach me for a better copy, and then sits and makes an objection and cross-examines the witness on a matter that isn't even the witness's responsibility for. Again, as I indicated earlier, if counsel would like to contact me, I will make arrangements to provide better copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, Your Honour, I have a different proposal. I will ask, since this witness is employed here in the Tribunal in the Office of the Prosecutor, we need a day or two to make a list of all the bad copies, and we'll make this list available to the Prosecutor so that he can provide us with a better copy or with originals, and then our cross-examination will make more sense, if that is indeed so, and if Mr. Prosecutor really has better copies. And the witness is here. He is always available, if I understood correctly. Because we have a lot of such documents. We will ask to be provided with better copies from the Prosecution for our own sake and for the sake of the Trial Chamber as well, of course. And then we'll proceed with cross-examination. Otherwise, we will be engaging in an exercise in futility. The logical thing to do would be to stop this now and ask for better copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I'm surprised to hear what you are saying to us. We had this witness last Wednesday, and we had two days for you to prepare your cross-examination. And you are not in the position to make this kind of request because you had those documents long before your cross-examination, and some even could date back before this trial. So you still need two days for this witness to be under the oath, and you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come back to cross-examine this witness. I'm very surprised to hear that. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply want to note for the record --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I simply want to note for the record my direct examination, 55 minutes. The cross-examination has now gone on for more than five hours, after this witness being specifically adjourned so counsel could prepare from last Wednesday. And now it is almost a week later. There has been ample opportunity for counsel to prepare. And as Mr. President just noted, many of these documents have been possessed by counsel since December 2000. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can I ask you a question. Am I correct in assuming that very few of these documents exist in the office of the OTP in their original form?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In fact, that you have received copies from verifiable sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the vast majority of instances, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that some of the original copies which you received from the various sources - and there are many sources - are, in fact, not very clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. It's true. It's absolutely true. There are some that the quality is poor. For instance, to give the Court an example, and you may be able to relate to this in your own experience, some of these old type of fax material with the pages, the print tends to fade over time. That's one example. So it is true, Your Honour. Some of the documents, even the best copy available to the OTP as provided by the various sources, in some instances, the copy is quite poor. However, as the witness said a moment ago, there are often many instances where if one goes to what we call the original, which is a bit of a misnomer, the original copy, if we can use that terminology, if we go to the original copy, it is very often the case that a much better copy or document can be obtained, and we have done that on many occasions. And again, if the Chamber wishes, would like some additional specific documents to be pursued, we're happy to do that. Obviously, we produced a large volume of documents in this case. We have tried to exercise some quality control. Obviously, we haven't done it perfectly. There is a huge volume of papers, as everyone knows. But if the Chamber has particular documents it would like us to pursue, obviously we are only too happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: My query was really to see how we can resolve the problem of Mr. Krsnik examining documents in their original form until it occurred to me that you don't have any originals. The Spanish army or the British army or United Nations or indeed the Bosnian government would have the originals, so there is no possibility of offering Mr. Krsnik an opportunity to examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Clark, you're right, there are a few -- I don't want to mislead the Chamber. There are a few instances where, for whatever reason, we have actually obtained some original documents, but the vast majority of the collection is the original -- first generation copy, if I can say it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 429, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My first question is: How was this document obtained from the BH government? That is, which institution in the BH government, which agency, was the source of this document? If you know that, of course.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is it part of your practice to have documents which do not have a delivery number, your own reference number?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: These are so-called admission stamps, stamps confirming admission of a certain document, or a number under which the certain document is logged in the book of documents received. This number is -- exists on number documents. It doesn't exist on others. I'm asking: Have you come across such documents which lack this number, in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if this has been explained before. I mentioned before the ERN number, which you can see in every piece of evidence. This is an individual number for every page of evidence. You can see that in the translations as well as in the originals. For example --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not what we are talking about. I'm not asking about the ERN number. I'm asking about the admission stamp made by this unit, affixed by this unit, here on the document, and it's called, "A list of soldiers of the Convicts Battalion who should receive apartments."

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The original stamp? Which stamp, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Here, in this spot, there should be a stamp confirming admission with a number under which this document is filed in the unit. I'll show you another document to clarify what I mean. Exhibit 492 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we have counsel testifying. There is no evidence in the record of what the normal HVO document practices were, and simply counsel's assertion. If he wants to call witnesses to that effect, he can do so, but he's simply asserting facts that are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please clear it up, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's precisely what I'm trying to do. I'm giving an example. For instance, document 492, it has in the heading, number 0021, followed by a certain text of the letterhead, and that's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You are testifying to the foundation for documents, and I'm asking you why is there no admission number on this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir; I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's the point. How can he address that? How can he say why some HVO document clerk did not put a document -- put that on this number? How can this witness say that? He can say -- we can all read the document and say, "I look at it now. I don't see that on the document." Now, the witness can do that, but he can't say why some office -- some officer, presumably some junior officer, of the Convicts Battalion, or clerk who made this list, he can't say why he didn't put this number on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was just about to give me an explanation. I really don't understand the anger of my learned friend from the Prosecution, because the witness said he had been studying documents from the archives, from all the other sources, that he had dealt with these documents, that he's familiar with them. And he's a witness for the Prosecution. He's here to clarify it for us and for you. I don't know who else to ask. And I believe that the witness has just started giving his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to understand the Chamber is also not very familiar with the format of those documents. And we believe that there is some reasonings behind the objections from the Prosecutor, but in this case, if the witness would like to answer the question, let him to answer your question, if he knows the answer. Yes, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are several points of interest for this Chamber in connection to this document. This document was submitted, was given to us, by the Bosnian authorities. Normally, it is often the case that these documents come from seizures that the Bosnian army did during the war. I believe that this is the case. As you may know, the Bosnian army seized the northern barracks of the HVO on the 30th of June of 1993, and they had the opportunity to seize some documents, the northern barracks as well as the area of Bijelo Polje, and that's how they could take -- they could seize documents of the 1st Battalion of the 2nd Brigade, which is the unit that was deployed in that particular area. That is the logical explanation for that. And that is the same case for some documents given to us by the Bosnian authorities from Doljani. In the same way, the Bosnian army managed to capture documents in Doljani. I believe that that happened in July 1993. And they delivered to us copies of those documents. That is how we have documents from those particular units and not from other units given by the Bosnian authorities. These we have been able to establish with the discussions and with the process of verification the authenticity of the documents. More. HVO units, normally, as were you saying, there was some truth in what you were saying; normally they do have a registration number. I was confused because you were referring to the stamp, which is something else. But there is such a, we can say, registration number or a serial number, so that the documents are registered in a logbook or in a registry book. That is a common procedure. So, as you were rightly saying, that is the case normally - not always, but normally - that is the regular procedure for documents issued by the main staff of the HVO. And that is how I could tell you yesterday that that was in fact a document of the main staff, because I could recognise the numbering system. As for the main staff of the HVO, we have also the logbooks, the registry books. So that's why I'm certain -- that's why I conclude that the document of the main staff that was presented yesterday is an authentic one. I have checked that against the registry book, against the logbook, and I have seen the entry. The entry says the number, the date, and the addressee of the document. This can be checked. This is -- if Trial Chamber finds this of interest, this can be checked against the logbook, the original logbooks. We don't have all of them, unfortunately, but we have a number of them. Let me tell you, this information is all available in the indexes of the state archive of Croatia. You can see the indexes. The staff of the Croatia archive has done a very professional job, very good job, and in the index you can find the logbooks, you can go to the logbook and you can verify yourselves if the logbook matches with the document itself. That is the regular procedure, that is right. Nevertheless, in the HVO, like in any other organisation, there were anomalies. Some subcommanders were not complying with such a duty, or the clerks or whoever was in charge of such duty would neglect it, and there is the case in which some documents do not have such registration number. I believe that's the reality. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation. And precisely for the sake of finding out what the reality is, I would like to ask you to look at this Croatian original. Is it a draft document? Is it a memo? Is it a completed document? Is it an effective HVO document? Because, you see, there is something crossed out here. And my last question: Could it be someone's forgery? For instance, a soldier who wanted to receive an apartment could have put his name on the list and forged his signature. That's precisely what I was going to ask you, and thank you for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, as with yesterday afternoon, we are back to asking for pure speculation. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, do you have any evidence to show this document is a forged document? You may ask the questions about authenticity of these documents but not come to the conclusions before your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, can you claim with certainty that this document is not a forgery? Do you have evidence to prove it is not?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with absolute certitude. That very rarely is the case. I think that most likely this is an authentic document. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, so there is no confusion on this point, absolute certainty is not the standard of admission in this Tribunal, as I'm sure the Chamber will know from the Rules of Evidence. It's up to the Chamber to decide, in the totality of the circumstances, ultimately, what has probative value and what weight to assign, but there is no requirement that any document be authenticated with what counsel said, absolute certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for reminding us of this point. Mr. Krsnik, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. If I may, please, have the document 565.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you first how this document came into your possession, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is stated in the list, in the schedule that you received. This was given to us by the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see in the left-hand top corner the fax number. Is that a facsimile number, 15th August, 1993? The time is indicated as well.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be a fax number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you see on the right-hand side, there is a page number. The first page is missing. You see P2, P3, P4. Then pages 5 and 6 are missing. And we have page 7. Do you know where the other pages are in order to have a complete document? Because it's for trial purposes. At least, that's -- it's a legal document; at least, that's what we concluded.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to take a brief look on the original, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, by the numbering of the pages, I believe there is no page missing here. You can see at the top right side that you have two numbering systems. I don't know if you can -- can you follow this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have one numbering series, which starts with P, P.2, and it follows. And then you have the other one, which is the normal one for fax transmissions, with a symbol and then 004. If you follow the 2 numbering series, I think that you can conclude that these four pages follow one next to the other, and I believe that the document is complete as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Distinguished colleague, I see there are -- I said there are pages 2, 3, and 4, and then 5 and 6 are missing. But this is a legal document, a legal act, something that we are familiar with. And then follows an explanation of three or four sentences, and then the last page 007, so the pages 005 and 006 must be missing. Tell me only if you know. If you don't, it doesn't matter. Tell me, please, do you --

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're making a statement. If the question is if I agree with such a statement, I do not agree with such a statement. Maybe there is a confusion between the original numbering and the numbering of the fax transmission. What I am saying is that if you read properly, if you see together the two numbering systems, you can see 004, 005. Then we cannot see the next number, and then the last one is 007. So we have that problem. We don't see the fax numbering in the third page. If you follow the P-dot numbering, P.2, P.3, P.4, then we can't see what is the last numbering of the last page, but we can see the fax numbering, which is 007. So if you see together the two numbering series, I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you can conclude that, in fact, these four pages come together and make together the whole of the document. That's what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I can agree with your thinking now that I heard your explanations. We were only concerned that this document explains a decision on custody, and it is illogical for it to be too short. But anyway, I agree with your explanation. Can a legal document, a court document, be without a signature and without a stamp of the court concerned? Because -- well, I'm getting used to this system. I mean a handwritten signature, not a typewritten signature. In our part of the world, you always have to have a handwritten signature. The name can be typed out on a computer or typewriter or whatever, but there needs to be a handwritten signature and, of course, the stamp of the court concerned affixed to the document.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's a requirement in most parts of the world, and I would consider this an anomaly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We will agree that there is no handwritten signature and there is no stamp of the court concerned.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree on that. I think that this is -- this seems to be an anomaly. In fact, my comment on this, my experience dealing with documents produced by HVO military or civilian authorities is there was a certain deal of amateurism. People that were not trained professionally, because of the circumstances of the war, took positions that were beyond their professional ability which had an effect on the quality of the war and the documents that they produced. I can agree with your earlier comment that documents of this kind should be longer. That's a reasonable expectation. That happens also with some HVO orders, which with regular proper training would be longer and better produced. But due to certain amateurism of the officers, you may find such anomalies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is the district military court in Mostar, the highest military institution, highest military court institution, because civilian institutions were not functioning. So this was the highest judicial institution that was operating?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you found these anomalies there as well, that court decision can be valid without a signature, without a stamp? Perhaps we haven't really understood each other. You see, I mean, a judgment, after all, is a judgment.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't a statement of yours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assist you with some comments. The original structures were affected by the war. Many people left the country. Many highly qualified professionals left the country. Others were dismissed because of their ethnic background, and that affected the quality of the work of these institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, can I intervene at this stage. I know it's about seven or eight weeks ago, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [redacted] If my memory serves me right --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, my sincere apologies. I think perhaps we should go to private session for this because I think we get very close to identifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I said he had a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The document is not under seal. If we could go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My final question: In 1997, you testified actually that you were in Bosnia, if I remember your direct examination well. That was your testimony, wasn't it, that in '97, you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, it was in '96. In '97, I joined the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of visiting courts in Mostar, Sarajevo, and, for example, to ask for documents that have to deal with judicial institutions? Did you get them actually in order to compare what the government gave you and what you would obtain from court archives?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, when I visited Bosnia before joining the Tribunal, certainly I wasn't interested in judicial matters as such. After I joined the Tribunal, it's a different situation. The problem is that the Office of the Prosecutor has requested repeatedly from the authorities of Croatia and the Croatian authorities in Bosnia a number of documents under cooperation. To the best of my knowledge, they have never been helpful. They have not responded to our requests, so there is basically no cooperation, no opportunity for us to get such cooperation from Croat authorities until there was some changes in the institutions of the Republic of Croatia recently, relatively recently. And with those changes, the new authorities did grant us access to the state archive of Croatia. So in short, the Office of the Prosecutor has great difficulty to have cooperation, to obtain cooperation from those authorities. Furthermore, I would like to say something else, which is that these -- I would not consider these a reliable source. The military court in Mostar, it's not what I would call an independent source, certainly. This is an institution that was cooperating and assisting to the HVO. And their main purpose - this is my assessment - was to assist the military effort of the HVO, which casts some doubts about the reliability, or their credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Colleague, you have just presented some very interesting thoughts. If I have understood you correctly, when talking about the government of BH, you're referring to the Muslims in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; when you're talking about the Croat authorities, you are referring to the Croats in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, problem is that there are some contradictions in the institutions of the federation and in the implementation of the institutional agreements, but I would prefer -- I would rather not comment on those matters. There are some contradictions in that issue, but this is political, institutional problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we were at the court in Mostar and they told us that all the documents were here in The Hague, all the material that we requested. That's why I asked you whether you were perhaps in court and whether you asked for any of this. I'm talking about the years when peace prevailed in Bosnia, in 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999, 2000. That's why I put that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to suggest we are getting very, very far afield. We could spend, undoubtedly, days talking about the problems in Bosnia post-Dayton and the fact that there continued to be, in fact, illegally, a number of parallel institutions, and, indeed even now, there are very senior Bosnian Croat officials, some of whom were kicked out of the presidency by the Office of the High Representative, who are calling for a completely separate entity and reject the legitimacy of the BiH government. Now, we can spend days talking about that and about the fact that there are still, to this day, parallel Bosnian Croat institutions and all that, but we will spend a great deal of time on that, and I think it's beyond the scope of this witness and beyond the scope of the authentication of these documents. I can also -- if the Chamber wishes to have a hearing on these matters, I would be happy to talk about my years of trying to obtain documents from the Bosnian Croat part of the federation. Years. I'll be happy to discuss that at length, but we don't need this witness here to do that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, please do allow me to respond to this speech made by the Prosecutor. Such statements in the courtroom of a world court are simply inaccurate and they cannot be put that way. The point is that Bosnia-Herzegovina is governed by a governor. If somebody is legally elected in an election in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the governor can overturn the result of this election. But this is something that doesn't belong to this courtroom. This is a debate that can be carried out elsewhere; in which direction democracy is moving in the world and the UN, et cetera. However, thank you for having allowed me to respond to the Prosecutor. I haven't got many other questions. I have only three or four left, which distinctly show how illogical some of these things are. I would like to ask for document 737 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my first question: As concerns such documents that are being produced in court, are the translations checked? You will agree with me that if a translation is not accurate, there can be major damage. As you can see in this document, the English version says, "Older than 25." If you look at the Croat version - of course, we checked that out properly - it says, "Up to the age of 25."

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Secondly, in addition to this translation --

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I cannot comment on issues of translation, frankly. I think this question should be addressed to the people in charge of translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As far as you're concerned, that pertains to any document, right? I mean the question of the translation and the original. You always read the English version, right, not the Croat original? You read the English translation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I normally read both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you - I do beg your pardon - what is the point of this document? Why is it here? Especially since it doesn't have a signature either. As far as I understood this, this is a professional unit Baja Kraljevic. Will you agree with me that interpreters -- that the translators cannot provide for an interpretation, explanation? So please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please? Because the interpreters do not have these documents, the interpreters repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The job of the translators is to put "ATJ," not to go into explanations. How come a translator would know that this is an anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question should be better addressed to the translators, but my assessment is that this is actually the right spelling of such an acronym. I have seen it repeatedly, and normally, in this context particularly as related to this unit, "ATJ" stands for "anti-terrorist unit." I think this is a correct translation and explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where is it that this information raised by Mr. Krsnik is not on the Bosnian Croat original? On 00495032, I can't -- seems to say rather clearly on the letterhead, "Anti-terrorist group, Baja Kraljevic," and it says that again in a box of information below that. So I'm not sure where counsel is finding the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very clear, Your Honours. Please look at the Croat original. "The professional unit, ATJ Baja Kraljevic." It doesn't say anything else. That's what the Croat original says. And now look a bit further on, and then the translators have added, "Anti-terrorist unit." And then further on, document 738, the very next document, 738, now it says, "ATG." And then what was added was, "Anti-terrorist group." In the Croat original, this does not exist. It just says, "Professional unit, ATG, Baja Kraljevic." And now look further on, Mr. Scott, and Your Honours. In the English original, the number is 248/94, 249/93. Are these the same documents, or are -- or is this a translation of another Croatian document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this goes back to the similar question that Judge Clark raised about a document some minutes ago. If counsel is seriously suggesting these documents -- that they are not accurately refer to the Baja Kraljevic ATG, if we are engaged in semantic exercises here, Your Honour, I respectfully submit it's a poor use of the Chamber's time. If Mr. Krsnik seriously wants to put to this witness that it should not be -- this is not the Baja Kraljevic ATJ or ATG, it is not the Baja Kraljevic anti-terrorist group, then put that very clearly and succinctly to this witness. Otherwise, Your Honour, we are wasting a great deal of time on these matters. Unless that's the case. If counsel seriously contends, and has a good-faith basis for doing so, that the document is not otherwise what it purports to be, if he has that basis, then by all means I give him full opportunity to attack the document. Otherwise, we are wasting a huge amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you have to ask direct questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I weren't interrupted that often. And I think that I have indeed established a logical sequence in my questions. Your Honours, this is quite difficult for me, but I do try to focus and I think I am focused, and this examination would not last that long otherwise. The witness said to me that we should put this question to the translators, and I am concerned about the translation of these documents, because somebody cannot just add things to these documents if they are not authorised to do so, because in that case, the documents get a completely different meaning. As for this particular document, I have no further questions, because the witness answered me that I should put a question to the translators. So I have raised my doubts, yes. The translations are such that they can cause great damage, because these are completely different situations. Now, document 738, "up to the age of 25," and "over the age of 25," we have clarified this, I think. If we have not, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe the witness would like to say something. Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the acronym ATJ, I think in fact there is some minor discrepancy, but I don't think this is important, frankly, because both denominations, anti-terrorist group, ATG, and anti-terrorist unit, ATJ, both were used for such units within the Convicts Battalion. I have seen several documents use both acronyms. I think that the discrepancy between the two is really not very important. They mean the same in this context; anti-terrorist group or anti-terrorist unit. It seems that the translator took some liberty on adding this comment, but I think this is the right comment. This is -- this is consistent with the reality. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Could you tell us how long you are going to last for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have - let me see - about five documents that we have selected as examples. I think I will take no more than half an hour. If I could ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to go into private session so that I could address Judge Clark in private session, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, sir, we are now dealing with Document 738. It's the document immediately following the previous one. We can look at the English version, the English translation, and the Croat translation. [In English] 738, yeah. [Interpretation] In the right-hand upper corner, it says English translation -- there is a number indicated; and in the Croatian document, it says reference number. In the English original, the registration number is 248/94, and in the Croatian document, the number is 249/93. Is this a translation of a different document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will need a few seconds, please. Well, first, I think that your observation is right. There is a discrepancy in the reference number in the original and in the translation. Now, if it is a translation of the same document, I will need to check this carefully. Sir, it seems to me that there is a discrepancy or a mistake, as you mentioned, in the translation, in the reference number, but the rest of the translation I believe is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm that the registration number is a designation of the document, of a certain document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the purpose is to identify the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Therefore, I'm asking on this English version, the registration number is a year older, although I do allow that as far as the contents is concerned, there is no discrepancy with the Croatian document. However, the registration number seems to indicate that it's a translation of a different document from year 1994.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me, was the source again the government of the Muslims of the Bosnian -- of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the Bosniaks of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of the copy in Bosnian language, that's right. The translation, no. The translation was done here, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, then, can you confirm that this document was signed, type-signed, by deputy commander, but there is no handwritten signature?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see? Yes. That's right. That's visible on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Generally speaking, did you find units where half of the members are highly ranked officers? This unit has 86 members, out of which 42 are highly ranked officers.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I would say that this is quite unusual. This doesn't seem to be very logical, but that can be the case in the context that I explained before, which is a certain amateurism by the commanders of certain units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you think it's logical for it to be signed by the person who is fifth on the list, lower ranked than the first two, who is, on top of that, the deputy commander? Do you find that logical?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think we are getting far afield into asking this witness to speculate about the HVO practices in this regard. I'd also remind the Chamber that one of the earlier witnesses in this case actually testified specifically to the fact that there were large number of senior officers in this unit, that, in fact, that people in Zagreb objected to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, will you please skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my final question: Here, the professional unit of Baja Kraljevic is referred to as an ATG, and again, it is a liberal interpretation of the translator. Regardless of the fact that we know what it is, and as my learned friend put it, we know it to be true, but it's a different issue whether the translator has the right to interpret a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, but again, two things. Again, it's not a question for this witness. I'm also informed - I've actually been informed during the break - that the practice, in fact the standing instructions to the translation unit, is if they come across abbreviations, based on their experience they believe to be the case, their instructions are to provide that information as much as possible. If there is then some question about that, they are to indicate with a question mark in brackets as to if that's the correct abbreviation or not. Now, that is apparently the practice of the translation unit. Whether that's true or not, whether counsel objects to that or not, it's not a question for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I also believe that it's not a question for this witness, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to move on to the next document, 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you? Witness, I have one question. Here we see the date of 8th March, 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, is this the signature of Mladen Naletilic himself? Of course, I'm asking your answer not as an expert, but you did say that you read both versions of the document and that you can find your way around both English and the Croatian version. Can you confirm to me that it's the signature of Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the quality is not very good, but I believe that that is right. This may be the case. Besides, I know that Ivan Andabak acted as a deputy of Mr. Naletilic, and there are a large number of documents in which we have seen that it is type-signed Mladen Naletilic and hand-signed Ivan Andabak. This may well be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How do you know that Ivan Andabak was the deputy of Mr. Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's what I have learned from the evidence available to the Prosecutor, primarily documentary evidence as well as statements of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, it says here, "Commander," and it's personally signed by Ivan Andabak. If it were a deputy commander, there should be the word "for," or "on behalf of."

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with due respect, I think that your observation is not right. It's typewritten "Commander" and type-signed "Mladen Naletilic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly. But it doesn't say "on behalf of" the commander or "for" the commander. When you sign something personally, it's the normal practice to add this. If Ivan Andabak signed it, it should have "on behalf of" or "for" added to the "Commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again we have counsel testifying. We don't know what Ivan Andabak's practice was; we don't know how he signed documents apparently for Mr. Tuta. I say that now because there are, indeed, a large number of documents in the record. But I don't think this witness can speculate as to what Ivan Andabak's signature practices were or whether he signed it in his own name or whether he put "on behalf of" or not. It doesn't say that, and everyone in the courtroom can look at the document and say, I don't see anything that has been interpreted "on behalf of" or "for." But I don't think, beyond that, this witness can speculate as to Ivan Andabak's signing practices. Perhaps Mr. Andabak should come as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we believe that document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have just one more question regarding this document. What was the source?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is stated in the schedule that you received, but we can check that. It seems that the source was the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have one more question still regarding this document. Do you have any evidence at all that Mr. Naletilic had knowledge about the existence of this document and the document signed by Mr. Andabak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I again object. Speculation. It goes beyond the scope of direct examination and the purpose of calling this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, it's really beyond the scope of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you say the government, I mean the Bosniaks in the BH federation, the source of this document precisely was the Agency for Investigations and Documentation or the Ministry of the Interior or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, frankly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can move on to document 778. Witness, first of all, can we agree that the Croatian version is illegible?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that the Croatian version, it's partly legible, that one can read about 80 per cent of the content. This issue has been raised before. What I can advise is that certainly if a translation was made by us, at some point there was available, or there is available, a sufficiently good copy. If the translator finds that the original, it's illegible, it will show in the translation, in between brackets, it will show "partly illegible" in the translation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you confirm that what we have here is a supplement to some previous statement that somebody gave to the Centre of Security Services in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the document states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that the previous statement is missing in this compilation of evidence? Or perhaps you have it at the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have not reviewed the whole collection, all the binders, so I cannot comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I didn't ask for your comment. I think my question was clear. Is this a supplement to some earlier statement? In order to understand the supplement, we need to have this earlier statement. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it is a supplementary statement, I already answered, yes. It seems to be so. That if you need or if you need the first statement, that's for you to assess. If the first statement is available in the collection, I don't know, because I have not reviewed the whole collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it is a statement or testimony given to the police in the Security Services Centre of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, you can see, this is visible from the document itself, it says, "Zenica Security Services, Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Such a statement was presented here as evidence, and such a statement given to the police cannot serve as evidence. The witness should be brought here. I don't know what you want to prove with this because that's a statement given to the police and the man --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm not sure how that's a question for this witness to answer. If Mr. Krsnik has a legal objection to this exhibit, he can address that to the Chamber, but I'm not sure how this witness can assist about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You have gone a little bit too far in this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to address you. With my questions that are constantly being restricted, I am trying, for our sake and for the sake of the Chamber, to make some things clear, because a statement was presented here and an attempt is being made to tender it into evidence. I think the witness should be brought here, because we don't have the earlier statement, we don't know what he originally stated, and that's all I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you want to do that, you have the full opportunity to ask this witness to be here as your own witness, to dispute this document. Mr. Krsnik, you may ask why the original statement is missing. I think this is a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have asked that question among the first questions I asked. I asked the witness whether he knows about that statement, where it is, whether they have it in their possession, and I think the witness answered. He said he didn't know, if I understood him. But I don't know what the basis is for introducing this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can you provide us with some information about the first statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll inquire. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can I ask you the same question that Mr. Krsnik is trying to put to the witness, and I, myself, am confused as to why the record of an interview with somebody is included in these documents. What is its probative value? It's an unusual document included in all the others, and I, myself, I have discussed it with other members of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's put in -- Your Honour, I understand the Chamber's concerns, and I would say it is, indeed, different than some of the other documents. It is, however, like many of the other HVO records or ABiH records, it's simply an historical report, just as there are a number of other historical reports by the HVO; report of an action, report of an incident. And this is just an historical document. It wasn't prepared for trial. It wasn't prepared for this case. We didn't ask anyone to prepare it. It was just an historical record of these -- of this matter. And we thought that since the content of it directly relates to matters in the case, that it might assist the Chamber. But I do understand -- I do understand -- I think I understand the Chamber's -- Judge Clark, your concerns. And I agree; it's a somewhat different type of document. But I think that's the only answer -- the best answer I can give the Chamber. I'm happy to look for the related statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we agree that your questioning in relation to this is extremely valid as to why is it included at all, and we'll give it a little more thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I would like us to move on to Document 654. Witness, could you please look at the last sentence, the last sentence, [In English] "... defence of Croatian territory battles up to now ..." And now we look at the Croatian original. In the Croatian original, it says quite clearly, and also in the spirit of the language quite explicitly, that it is "... the defence of Croat territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." On the basis of the English translation, one would think that it were the defence of the Croatian State, to radically explain what all of this is about.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is exactly the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would suggest that the translation -- if there's a dispute about translation, maybe the booth can simply translate that sentence on the bottom of the B/C/S original for us, and simply -- I think that's the best answer, if there's a translation question. I don't see -- I admit not speaking B/C/S, but when I look at the B/C/S original, I don't see anything in there that suggests that it makes reference to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you may read the original documents in the B/C/S. Let's hear what the translation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. This is a question that is very sensitive because it has to do with a pistol that is being awarded by a minister, the minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And he submits his proposal to the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. That is why this is an extremely sensitive question, and now I'm going to read the sentence in the Croatian language. So there was a list of names. "All the mentioned persons are members of the Convicts Battalion, and they gave an outstanding contribution to the defence of Croat territories in the previous battles." So above Award, or Accord, it says: "On the basis of Article 30, paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4 of the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Narodne List number 6/92. I propose that you award ..." My question is very clear: Is this being awarded on the basis of a contribution that was given for a struggle that was waged in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, on the basis of the English translation, as we understood it, is it being accorded for the Defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's argumentative. The literal translation is, as by the interpretation booth just now, was Croatian territory. Now, that can mean a lot of different things perhaps to different people, and one could argue in this case that it means something quite specific about the claims to this particular part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that in fact was -- this was considered Croatian territory. Now, I don't want to argue that point now, but that's exactly my point; it's argumentative for counsel to put that to the witness. We've had the literal translation of the document, and that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I omitted -- of course, interpreters cannot testify in court, but my learned friend doesn't know the Croat language and syntax of the Croatian language. In the Croat original, "Croat territories" is written with a small letter "H," "hrvatski territorija," whereas if we were speaking about the Republic of Croatia, then the noun "Croatia" would have to be spelled with a capital "H," "Hrvatski." This is something that we studied in primary school, so we all know this. And this is the rule that I am invoking, Mr. Scott. And I have really focused on my questions and my concentration is being broken all the time and I'm really asking my learned friend to let me finish the cross-examination of this witness. If the witness does not know how to answer these questions, then he can say so himself. But this explanation was necessary because I'm just trying to point out to the Trial Chamber of how many problems are included in these documents; the language itself, the numbers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the points expressed by both parties have been correctly recorded in the transcript. Let's hear the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. From the text of the document, it can be interpreted both ways. This is ambiguous. It could have been in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or it could have been in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.
